questions.prompt: How does machine learning differ from traditional rule-based programming?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Instead of a human writing explicit rules, the computer learns patterns from example data

Traditional programming means a human writes the rules directly; machine learning learns the rules (or the pattern connecting inputs to outputs) from many examples instead.
keyPoints: Traditional programming means a human writes the rules directly; machine learning learns the rules (or the pattern connecting inputs to outputs) from many examples instead.

questions.prompt: What is the validation set used for during model development?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Comparing models and tuning settings (hyperparameters) before the final evaluation

The validation set lets you compare different models or settings and pick the best one, while keeping the test set completely untouched for one final, honest evaluation.
keyPoints: The validation set lets you compare different models or settings and pick the best one, while keeping the test set completely untouched for one final, honest evaluation.

questions.prompt: What problem does regularization primarily help address?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Overfitting — by discouraging overly large weights that make a model too sensitive to training data

Regularization adds a penalty for large weights during training, nudging the model toward simpler solutions that are less likely to overfit the training data's noise.
keyPoints: Regularization adds a penalty for large weights during training, nudging the model toward simpler solutions that are less likely to overfit the training data's noise.

questions.prompt: What's the core idea behind a random forest?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Training many different decision trees and combining their predictions, which reduces overfitting compared to any single tree

A random forest builds an ensemble of many trees, each trained slightly differently, and combines their predictions — this averaging cancels out much of the overfitting any individual tree would show on its own.
keyPoints: A random forest builds an ensemble of many trees, each trained slightly differently, and combines their predictions — this averaging cancels out much of the overfitting any individual tree would show on its own.

questions.prompt: How does KNN make a prediction for a new data point?
questions.referenceAnswer: KNN finds the k nearest training examples to the new point (by distance) and bases its prediction on those neighbors' labels — majority vote for classification, average for regression.
keyPoints: KNN finds the k nearest training examples to the new point (by distance) and bases its prediction on those neighbors' labels — majority vote for classification, average for regression.

choices.text: By fitting a line through all the training data
By looking at the k closest training points and taking their majority vote or average
By building a decision tree
By computing gradients and updating weights

questions.prompt: Why can a single train/validation split give a misleading picture of model performance?
questions.referenceAnswer: A model's measured performance can shift noticeably depending on which particular rows ended up in the validation set — cross-validation averages over many different splits to reduce this luck-of-the-draw effect.
keyPoints: A model's measured performance can shift noticeably depending on which particular rows ended up in the validation set — cross-validation averages over many different splits to reduce this luck-of-the-draw effect.

choices.text: Single splits are always exactly accurate
The specific rows that happen to land in each set can make a model look better or worse than it truly is, especially with smaller datasets
Single splits can't be used to evaluate models at all
There's no real risk with a single split

questions.prompt: When might MAE be preferred over RMSE for evaluating a regression model?
questions.referenceAnswer: MAE treats all errors proportionally to their size, without the extra penalty for large errors that squared-error-based metrics like RMSE apply — useful when big and small errors are roughly equally undesirable.
keyPoints: MAE treats all errors proportionally to their size, without the extra penalty for large errors that squared-error-based metrics like RMSE apply — useful when big and small errors are roughly equally undesirable.

choices.text: When large errors should be punished much more heavily than small ones
When every unit of error should be weighted roughly equally, without disproportionately punishing occasional large misses
MAE should never be used in practice
When the target variable is categorical

questions.prompt: What's a key advantage of hierarchical clustering over k-means?
questions.referenceAnswer: Hierarchical clustering builds a full tree of nested groupings, letting you decide how many clusters to use by cutting the tree at different levels after the fact, rather than committing to k upfront.
keyPoints: Hierarchical clustering builds a full tree of nested groupings, letting you decide how many clusters to use by cutting the tree at different levels after the fact, rather than committing to k upfront.

choices.text: It always runs faster than k-means
You don't need to choose the number of clusters before running it — you can decide after seeing the full dendrogram
It never requires any parameters to be set
It can only be used on text data

questions.prompt: A classifier has high accuracy but misses nearly every rare positive. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Inspect class prevalence and the confusion matrix. Measure precision and recall for the positive class. Choose a decision threshold using the operational cost of errors.
keyPoints: Inspect class prevalence and the confusion matrix.
Measure precision and recall for the positive class.
Choose a decision threshold using the operational cost of errors.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Choose a decision threshold using the operational cost of errors. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Choose a decision threshold using the operational cost of errors.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Inspect class prevalence and the confusion matrix. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Inspect class prevalence and the confusion matrix.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
